topic: Why AI alone won't grow your LinkedIn, and how to use it well: give before you take, break your own patterns, better visuals, a steady rhythm, the audience you want, and prompts for drafting in your own voice
audience: Professionals who post on LinkedIn (or want to) and have started using AI to write their posts, but feel their posts sound like everyone else's and go nowhere
goal: Stop handing the whole post to AI; use it to sharpen their own ideas, plan visuals and keep a steady rhythm, with copy-ready prompts that keep the writing in their own voice
notes: Mojeed Abisiga is a data and AI leader and educator whose mission is to make data and AI easy for everyone; he teaches people to use AI at work, founded DataGlobal Hub and is a Forbes Technology Council member. [https://mojeedabisiga.com/]

LinkedIn's Help Center says your feed contains insights from your network, companies you follow, sponsored content, and other posts LinkedIn believes you may be interested in. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a523360]

To decide what to recommend, LinkedIn considers whether content is high quality and professionally relevant, whether it is relevant to all members, and your feedback, such as disinterest signals and content reports. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a523360]

LinkedIn says the feed evaluates three main types of signals: Identity (profile details such as location, workplace and skills), Content, and Activity. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1339724]

Content signals LinkedIn lists include how often a post is viewed or engaged with, what it is about and whether it provides knowledge or advice, how recent it is, its language, how constructive or professional the conversation is, and tagged people, companies or topics. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1339724]

Activity signals LinkedIn lists include what you've reacted to, commented on or shared, who you interact with frequently or recently, content you spend the most time viewing, and the engagement others have with your posts and how recent it is. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1339724]
LinkedIn says its feed algorithms filter out or taper distribution of low-quality and unsafe content. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1339724]

On 12 March 2026 LinkedIn announced it is upgrading feed ranking with larger sequence models called Generative Recommenders, augmented with LLMs, using signals you choose to share (industry, skills, experience, geography) alongside how you engage over time. [https://news.linkedin.com/2026/ImprovingTheFeed]
LinkedIn says it takes action against comment automation, engagement pods and unauthorized third-party tools that create inauthentic engagement. [https://news.linkedin.com/2026/ImprovingTheFeed]
LinkedIn says it is showing less engagement bait and recycled content, such as 'comment to agree' prompts or videos that don't match the text. [https://news.linkedin.com/2026/ImprovingTheFeed]

LinkedIn Engineering (12 March 2026) says the new ranking system uses profile information you've chosen to share (industry, experience, skills, geography) and how you engage over time, including what you've read, liked, commented on, returned back to, or simply scrolled past. [https://www.linkedin.com/blog/engineering/feed/engineering-the-next-generation-of-linkedins-feed]

LinkedIn Engineering says its new retrieval system, built on LLM-generated embeddings, surfaces content from authors you don't follow. [https://www.linkedin.com/blog/engineering/feed/engineering-the-next-generation-of-linkedins-feed]

For each post, the model's input includes the post format, author information (name, headline, company, industry), engagement counts, article metadata and the post text. [https://www.linkedin.com/blog/engineering/feed/engineering-the-next-generation-of-linkedins-feed]

LinkedIn posts can contain up to 3,000 characters, and you can save a post as a draft and keep editing it later, including from another device. Longer than that, LinkedIn suggests writing an article on its Publishing Platform. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a528176]

On desktop, click 'Start a post', then the name dropdown to set 'Who can see your post?' (Anyone, Connections only, or Group) and 'Who can comment on your post?' (Anyone, Connections only, or Off). [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a528176]

The post composer can add emojis, a photo or video, an event or a celebration, and under the Plus icon: share that you're hiring, create a poll, add a document, or Services. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a528176]
To schedule a post, click the Clock icon in the composer and pick a date and time; scheduled posts are managed from the post composer. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a528176]

LinkedIn may limit the visibility of posts when it detects excessive posting that indicates inauthentic activity or an automation tool, and may cap posts per time period. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a528176]

Document posts accept PPT, PPTX, DOC, DOCX and PDF files up to 100MB and 300 pages; after uploading you can edit the description but not the document, and viewers can download it as a PDF. LinkedIn advises converting files to PDF where possible. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a518909]

LinkedIn's 'Best practices for content created with the help of AI' says it does not want 'AI slop': low-effort, likely AI-generated content that sounds polished but lacks a clear point of view, unique perspective or substance. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1481496]

LinkedIn says it judges whether content adds value, not how it was made: AI-assisted content is welcome when it reflects a real person's perspective, while generic or repetitive content is less likely to be widely distributed. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1481496]

LinkedIn urges members to review, edit and approve AI-assisted content, says you are responsible for everything you post, and recommends saying so when you relied heavily on AI (if it isn't obvious). [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1481496]

Members can flag a post or comment via the More menu > 'Seems like AI slop'; if a post gets enough such feedback its author sees a tip in Post analytics, which LinkedIn says is not a takedown or policy decision. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1481496]

With the creator mode change, the profile's Connect button becomes Follow, your follower count shows in your introduction, and you can choose Follow or Connect as your primary action. [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a5999182]

Creator analytics (combined post and audience analytics) are reached from the Analytics section of your profile or by selecting the Post impressions count on the left pane of your feed (help page last updated about two years ago; the location may have changed). [https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a5999182]

In Claude, project instructions apply only to chats within that project; projects are self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories and knowledge bases, available to all users. [https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10185728-understanding-claude-s-personalization-features] [https://support.claude.com/en/articles/9517075-what-are-projects]
